reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: A mosquito-borne flavivirus maintained in a bird reservoir with Culex mosquitoes as the main vector; humans are incidental dead-end hosts
The large majority of infections are asymptomatic, and most symptomatic cases present as a self-limiting febrile illness (West Nile fever) with headache, myalgia, and sometimes a transient rash
A small proportion develop neuroinvasive disease: meningitis, encephalitis, or an acute flaccid paralysis resembling poliomyelitis
Advancing age and immunosuppression are the strongest risk factors for severe neuroinvasive disease
Acute flaccid paralysis from anterior horn cell involvement is an important clue that distinguishes WNV from many other causes of encephalitis
Transmission can also occur through blood transfusion and organ transplantation, so donor screening is relevant in endemic areas
Management is supportive; there is no specific licensed antiviral therapy, and prevention centres on mosquito control and personal protection
reference.pathophysiology: West Nile virus is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus circulating between birds and Culex mosquitoes. After a mosquito bite the virus replicates locally and in regional lymph nodes, producing viraemia. In a minority of hosts it crosses into the central nervous system, where it infects neurons, particularly in the brainstem, deep grey matter, and anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, producing encephalitis and flaccid paralysis. Host factors such as age and immune status strongly influence whether infection stays confined to a febrile illness or becomes neuroinvasive.
additionalDifferentials: Other arboviral encephalitides (Japanese encephalitis, St Louis encephalitis)
Guillain-Barre syndrome (for the flaccid paralysis presentation)
Dengue or other acute febrile arboviral illness
infectionMimics: Poliomyelitis and other causes of acute flaccid paralysis
additionalInvestigations: CSF examination showing a lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein in neuroinvasive disease
WNV-specific IgM in serum and CSF (mainstay of diagnosis), with paired serology for confirmation
Nucleic acid testing in early infection or in immunocompromised or transfusion/transplant-associated settings
MRI of the brain and spinal cord to evaluate encephalitis and anterior horn involvement
Testing to exclude treatable causes such as herpes simplex and bacterial meningitis
redFlags: Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal neurological signs indicating encephalitis
Acute flaccid limb weakness suggesting anterior horn cell involvement
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem dysfunction
Severe disease in an elderly or immunocompromised patient with rapid deterioration
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated West Nile fever resolves fully, but neuroinvasive disease carries substantial morbidity and mortality, and survivors of encephalitis or flaccid paralysis may be left with long-lasting neurological and functional deficits, particularly older patients.
pitfalls: Assuming a benign viral illness and missing early neuroinvasive features in an older patient
Failing to distinguish WNV flaccid paralysis from Guillain-Barre syndrome, which has different management
Not considering transfusion- or transplant-associated transmission in a recently exposed patient
Delaying empirical treatment for herpes simplex encephalitis while awaiting WNV confirmation
management: With no proven specific antiviral, manage symptomatic disease supportively with fluids, antipyretics and analgesia
Admit neuroinvasive disease for supportive neurological care, seizure control and close monitoring
Provide respiratory support, including mechanical ventilation, for acute flaccid paralysis with diaphragmatic or bulbar involvement
Give empirical aciclovir and antibacterials until herpes simplex encephalitis and bacterial meningitis are excluded
Refer survivors with residual deficits for neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy and occupational therapy
Apply public health measures including mosquito-bite avoidance, vector control and blood and organ donor screening in endemic areas
Escalate to intensive care for respiratory failure or deteriorating encephalitis, particularly in older or immunosuppressed patients
